frenchConcept: All nouns in French are either Masculine (un/le) or Feminine (une/la). Adjectives must agree in gender and number.
englishAnalogy: English lost grammatical gender centuries ago, so English-only speakers struggle with this. Memorize nouns strictly with their article (un/une, le/la).
spanishAnalogy: Direct 1-to-1 match with Spanish! Almost all Spanish -o masculine and -a feminine nouns match French gender (el libro -> le livre, la mesa -> la table).
teluguAnalogy: Unlike Telugu which uses natural gender (Mahat/Mahati vs Neut/Achethana), French forces gender onto inanimate things. Do not think in Telugu neuter terms.
hindiAnalogy: Identical to Hindi! In Hindi, inanimate objects have grammatical gender (कमरा m, किताब f) and adjectives change accordingly (बड़ा कमरा, बड़ी किताब).
exampleFrench: Un grand livre (m) / Une grande table (f)
exampleEnglish: A big book (no gender) / A big table
exampleSpanish: Un gran libro (m) / Una gran mesa (f)
exampleTelugu: ఒక పెద్ద పుస్తకం / ఒక పెద్ద బల్ల (లింగ భేదం లేదు)
exampleHindi: एक बड़ा कमरा (m) / एक बड़ी किताब (f)
practicalTip: Never memorize a French noun in isolation. Always learn the article attached: 'une table', 'un stylo'.

topic: Formal vs Informal Pronouns of Address (Tu vs Vous)
frenchConcept: French strictly distinguishes informal 'Tu' (friends, kids, peers) from formal/plural 'Vous' (strangers, elders, officials, examiners).
englishAnalogy: English uses generic 'you' for everyone. English speakers often accidentally offend examiners by using 'Tu' in formal Section A tasks.
spanishAnalogy: Direct 1-to-1 match with Spanish: Tu = Tú (informal) and Vous = Usted (formal).
teluguAnalogy: Exact 1-to-1 match with Telugu: 'Tu' = నువ్వు (Nuvvu) and 'Vous' = మీరు (Meeru). Mixing them up causes immediate social awkwardness.
hindiAnalogy: Exact 1-to-1 match with Hindi: 'Tu' = तू / तुम and 'Vous' = आप. Mixing them up causes offense just like in Hindi.
exampleFrench: Comment vous appelez-vous ? (Formal) vs Comment tu t'appelles ? (Informal)
exampleEnglish: What is your name? (Identical for everyone in English)
exampleSpanish: ¿Cómo se llama usted? (Formal) vs ¿Cómo te llamas? (Informal)
exampleTelugu: మీ పేరు ఏమిటి? (మీరు) vs నీ పేరు ఏమిటి? (నువ్వు)
exampleHindi: आपका नाम क्या है? (आप) vs तेरा/तुम्हारा नाम क्या है? (तू/तुम)
practicalTip: In TEF Section A (Inquiry), you MUST use VOUS (మీరు/Usted). In Section B (Persuasion with a friend), you MUST use TU (నువ్వు/Tú).

topic: Nasal Vowels & Dental Consonants (an, in, on, un)
frenchConcept: Nasal vowels (an, in, on, un) require air to escape simultaneously through nose and mouth without touching the tongue to the roof of the mouth.
englishAnalogy: English vowel sounds are fully oral, causing English speakers to clumsily pronounce the 'N' consonant at the end.
spanishAnalogy: Spanish consonants /t/ and /d/ are already dental (identical to French). French nasal vowels are unique and must resonate in the nasal cavity.
teluguAnalogy: Dental T/D in French are identical to Telugu దంత్య త/ద (tongue on front teeth), never retroflex ట/డ. Nasal vowels resonate like తెలుగు అనునాసికాలు.
hindiAnalogy: Identical to Hindi Chandrabindu (माँ, चाँद, आँख). French T/D are dental (दंत्य त/द), exactly like Hindi.
exampleEnglish: A good white wine (Pronounced with hard 'n' in English)
exampleSpanish: Un buen vino blanco (Dental t/d match French)
exampleHindi: माँ, चाँद की तरह अनुनासिक ध्वनि (माँ = /mɑ̃/)
practicalTip: Hold your nostrils lightly while practicing: you should feel a vibration during nasal vowels (an/on/in).

frenchConcept: Passé Composé is for completed, punctual actions. Imparfait is for background setting, recurring habits, or ongoing states.
englishAnalogy: Similar to 'I ate / I was eating' or 'I used to eat'. Imparfait sets the scenery; Passé Composé narrates the main events.
spanishAnalogy: Direct parallel with Spanish Pretérito Perfecto/Indefinido vs Pretérito Imperfecto (comí vs comía).
teluguAnalogy: Imparfait = ongoing state/habit (చేస్తూ ఉండేవాడిని / జరిగింది). Passé Composé = single finished action (నేను తిన్నాను / చేశాను).
hindiAnalogy: Imparfait = background habit (मैं करता था / हो रहा था). Passé Composé = punctual action (मैंने किया / हुआ).
exampleFrench: Pendant que je dormais (Imp), le téléphone a sonné (PC).
exampleEnglish: While I was sleeping (Imp), the phone rang (PC).
exampleHindi: जब मैं सो रहा था (Imp), फ़ोन बजा (PC).
practicalTip: Ask yourself: Is this a clock-time event (Passé Composé) or a continuous backdrop/habit (Imparfait)?

frenchConcept: Subjunctive expresses subjective mood (necessity, doubt, emotion, wish: 'Il faut que...') rather than objective reality.
englishAnalogy: English barely retains subjunctive ('I insist that he be present'). In French, it is grammatically mandatory after specific triggers.
spanishAnalogy: Exact 1-to-1 match with Spanish Subjuntivo! Triggers and usage mirror Spanish (Es necesario que haga -> Il faut que je fasse).
teluguAnalogy: Expresses necessity or intent (అవసరం, సంకల్పం: 'ఇలా జరగాల్సి ఉంది / చేయాల్సి ఉంటుంది') rather than a simple statement of fact.
hindiAnalogy: Expresses necessity or desire ('यह ज़रूरी है कि वह करे'). Used in dependent clauses.
exampleEnglish: It is necessary that you come.
practicalTip: Memorize the top 5 B2 triggers: 'Il faut que...', 'Bien que...', 'Pour que...', 'Avant que...', 'Je crains que...'.

frenchConcept: Over 35% of English words and 70%+ of Spanish words derive from Norman French and Latin roots.
englishAnalogy: Direct transfer: -tion words (Condition -> Condition), -able (Comfortable -> Confortable), -ty -> -té (Liberty -> Liberté), -ly -> -ment.
spanishAnalogy: Massive lexical crossover: Spanish and French share thousands of cognates (nación -> nation, difícil -> difficile, posibilidad -> possibilité).
teluguAnalogy: Use your English and Spanish vocabulary as a massive shortcut to read advanced French articles without translating word-for-word.
hindiAnalogy: Use English Latin words as a direct shortcut to read B2 journalistic texts rapidly.
exampleFrench: La situation économique est très difficile.
exampleEnglish: The economic situation is very difficult.
exampleSpanish: La situación económica es muy difícil.
practicalTip: When reading B1/B2 texts, guess meaning using English/Spanish Latin roots before checking a dictionary.
